    Imperial Palace East Gardens (皇居東御苑)

    Yasukuni Shrine (靖國神社)

    The 1869 Shintō shrine to Japan's war dead — great torii, cherry-tree avenue and the Yūshūkan war museum; politically contested, historically essential.

How we choose

Every place is recommended by named sources (review-aggregator star ratings never count as the recommender), pinned to its door from a published coordinate, and status-checked. Closed places stay, flagged, so you know they’re gone.

Must see
The places to plan a visit around — graded within each area, not across the city.
Worth the detour
Strong picks, worth going out of your way for.
Deep cut
For the curious: smaller, odder, more local.

Within each area, places are ordered by tier, then by number of named sources — never by popularity. No ratings, prices or opening hours are shown, because the guide doesn’t hold verified ones.

263 sights and 225 places to eat across Tokyo, organised the way Tokyoites think about the city — the big special wards (Chiyoda, Chūō, Minato, Shinjuku, Shibuya, Taitō, Sumida-Kōtō) as their own areas, the rest by the old compass terms Jōnan, Jōsai, Jōhoku and Jōtō, then the Tama hills and the Kantō day-trip ring (Kamakura, Hakone, Nikkō, Kawagoe, Fuji Five Lakes, Yokohama). The food list starts from what is Tokyo's own — Kanda soba, Edomae sushi and unagi, monjayaki, dozeu loach, yōshoku omurice, tonkatsu and shōyu ramen — with the Michelin bench and century-old shinise beside each other. Every place is traceable to its source.

How this guide was made

How the cuisine filters were policed

Every food card names a specific dish — a label alone doesn’t qualify. A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it serves. Tabelog and Retty scores may measure popularity but never count as a source.

Web-searched in Japanese and English, fact-checked

Every place is traceable to two credible sources, or a lone Michelin / UNESCO / Agency for Cultural Affairs designation — recorded in data/sources.json. Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked open. Yelp/TripAdvisor/Tabelog never count toward the two-source bar.

Why the areas look the way they do

Tokyo has no boroughs; its 23 special wards (tokubetsu-ku) are the equivalent. The seven densest get their own area; the other sixteen are grouped by the long-standing compass terms Jōnan (south: Shinagawa, Meguro, Ōta), Jōsai (west: Setagaya, Nakano, Suginami), Jōhoku (north: Toshima, Bunkyō, Kita, Arakawa, Itabashi, Nerima) and Jōtō (east: Katsushika, Edogawa, Adachi). Every place is filed by the ward its address names.

What is thin, and why

Pins come only from published coordinates (Michelin venue pages, Wikipedia/Wikidata) — never from a map viewport or a ward centroid — so some well-sourced restaurants wait off the map until a place pin is found. The Tama and Kantō food lists are thin for that reason; it is stated here rather than filled with weaker picks.
